why: Section 11.9 fixes the size window directly: a true solution contains "solute particles with diameter in the range 0.1 to 2 nm", while colloids "contain particles of dispersed phase with diameters in the range at 2 to 500 nm". Converting, the colloidal range is \(2 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}\) to \(5 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}\), and the only printed interval that contains the whole of it is \(10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}\) to \(10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}\). Testing the others: \(10^{-10}\)–\(10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}\) is 0.1–1 nm, which is the true-solution range of a typical ion or small molecule, i.e. below colloidal dimensions; \(10^{-6}\)–\(10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}\) is 1–100 \(\mu\mathrm{m}\) and \(10^{-5}\)–\(10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}\) is larger still, both far above the 500 nm ceiling — particles that size settle on standing and belong to a suspension, whereas the chapter says colloids "do not separate on standing". The correct interval is therefore \(10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}\) to \(10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}\).

Gum is one of the chapter's own colloid examples — Table 11.6 lists "Sols of starch, gum" among the negatively charged sols — so the system is a sol, not a molecular dispersion. Which kind of sol follows from section 11.9.2 (b): lyophilic colloids are those "in which the particles of dispersed phase have a great affinity for the dispersion medium", and Table 11.5 records that they are "formed easily by direct mixing", are reversible and are self-stabilised. Gum swells and disperses in water on simple mixing and the sol is stable without any added stabiliser, which is exactly this description; being a macromolecule it is also a macromolecular colloid of the kind listed in section 11.9.2 (c) alongside starch and cellulose. Testing the others: it is not a true solution, because a true solution has particles of 0.1–2 nm and shows no Tyndall effect, while a gum sol scatters light; it is not a suspension, since suspension particles settle on standing and a gum sol does not; and it is not lyophobic, because the chapter's lyophobic examples are Ag, Au, hydroxides such as \(\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}\) and \(\mathrm{Fe(OH)_3}\) and metal sulfides, which are "formed only by special methods" and need traces of stabilisers. Gum in water is thus a lyophilic sol.

Section 11.7.2 gives the Haber process as its first example of heterogeneous catalysis, \(\mathrm{N_2(g)} + 3\,\mathrm{H_2(g)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{K_2O,\ Al_2O_3}]{\mathrm{Fe(s)}} 2\,\mathrm{NH_3(g)}\), and states in the next sentence: "Here \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) and \(\mathrm{K_2O}\) are promoters of the Fe catalyst … \(\mathrm{K_2O}\) causes chemisorption of nitrogen atoms." Testing the others: the catalyst itself is finely divided iron, and \(\mathrm{K_2O}\) only raises its activity rather than acting on its own; an inhibitor is defined in section 11.7.3 as a substance that decreases the rate of a chemical reaction, which is the opposite of what a promoter does; and the adsorbate is the species that accumulates on the catalyst surface — here the reactant nitrogen — whereas \(\mathrm{K_2O}\) is part of the solid catalyst bed. \(\mathrm{K_2O}\) therefore acts as a promotor.

Table 11.4 classifies colloids by the physical states of the two phases, and the row for a liquid dispersed in a solid is named "gel", with the examples "cheese, butter, jellies". Fruit jam is a jelly: the fruit juice is trapped as the dispersed liquid inside a continuous solid pectin network, so it holds its shape instead of flowing. Testing the others: a sol in the same table is a solid dispersed in a liquid, the reverse arrangement; an emulsion is a liquid dispersed in another immiscible liquid (section 11.9.7, examples milk and hair cream), and jam has a solid, not a liquid, dispersion medium; and a true solution would be a single homogeneous transparent phase with particles of 0.1–2 nm, whereas jam is visibly heterogeneous and semi-solid. Fruit jam is therefore a gel.
